args.body:
REDLINE REVIEW MEMORANDUM
Investment Advisory Agreement — Counterparty Markup
Funds & Asset Management Practice

PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
Prepared for: Client Engagement Team
Matter: Analyze Counterparty Markup of Investment Advisory Agreement
Deliverable: redline-review-memorandum.docx

I. SCOPE AND PURPOSE

We have reviewed the counterparty's latest markup of the Investment Advisory Agreement (the "Redlined Agreement") against the firm standard form and internal playbook, read together with the base deal materials, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and the controlling partner instructions. This memorandum identifies every deviation introduced by the counterparty, reconciles each against the firm's standard position and the applicable regulatory framework, and sets out a recommended accept / reject / counter position for each.

The deliverable addresses the operative record for this engagement. The matter folder also contains misfiled correspondence from an unrelated engagement (an administrative file concerning scheduling and invoice reconciliation for a different client); that file is not part of this matter and has not been relied upon in this analysis. The operative, controlling sources are the base deal materials, the counterparty markup, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and the partner deal correspondence (latest message controlling).

II. GOVERNING FRAMEWORK AND CONTROLLING SOURCES

A. Base materials and firm standard. The operative agreement (as negotiated between the parties) contains representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions. The firm standard form establishes the benchmark against which the counterparty's divergences are measured. Under the internal playbook, any deviation that materially enlarges the counterparty's rights or narrows our client's protections is presumptively disfavored unless affirmatively conceded by the client team.

B. Disclosure schedules and exhibits. The disclosure schedules qualify the base materials and, per the governing instruction, "control over general statements" in the base materials. Three scheduled items are dispositive for this review:
   • Schedule 3.7 — discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup's Material Adverse Effect (MAE) carve-outs;
   • Schedule 5.2 — lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift;
   • Exhibit B — sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts.

C. Controlling partner instruction. The latest message in the partner deal-communication thread revises the analysis priorities and controls over all earlier messages. The client will (i) concede the conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket, but (ii) treats any reduction in the survival period for the core representations as a walk-away issue. The deliverable reflects this controlling instruction and not the superseded priority ordering stated in earlier messages.

III. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS

The counterparty markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three deviations. Each is reconciled below against the base materials, the schedules/exhibits, and the controlling instruction.

DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification cap reduced; basket converted from deductible to tipping basket

Description. The counterparty silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the indemnification basket from a deductible (a true threshold, where recoveries begin only after the basket is exceeded in full) to a tipping basket (where, once the threshold is reached, all losses — including those below the threshold — become recoverable).

Reconciliation. The reduction of the cap, if adopted, would depress the maximum recovery otherwise available to our client. It also collides with Schedule 5.2, which lists retained liabilities. Reducing the cap in the very areas where retained liabilities are disclosed would silently shift a portion of those liabilities onto our client, because the cap would be reached sooner relative to the scheduled exposures. Schedule 5.2 qualifies the base materials and controls over general statements; the cap reduction is inconsistent with the retained-liability profile disclosed there.

The basket conversion is analytically distinct. A tipping basket is favorable to the buyer/indemnified party (it allows recovery of the full amount once the threshold is crossed) and unfavorable to the indemnifying counterparty. On its own, converting from a deductible to a tipping basket improves our client's position.

Recommended position.
   • Cap reduction: REJECT. The counterparty's silent reduction of the indemnification cap is inconsistent with the firm standard and would undermine the retained-liability protections reflected in Schedule 5.2. Counter with the firm-standard cap.
   • Basket conversion (deductible → tipping): CONCEDE in accordance with the controlling partner instruction. This change favors our client and the client team has directed that it be conceded. No further negotiation required on this element.

DEVIATION 2 — MAE definition adds carve-outs for regulatory action

Description. The counterparty amends the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" to add carve-outs excluding regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter."

Reconciliation. This deviation is material and must be assessed against Schedule 3.7, which discloses two pending regulatory inquiries relevant to this engagement. Because the proposed carve-out exempts regulatory action of exactly the kind already subject to two pending inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7, the carve-out, if accepted, would operate to strip the client of MAE protection precisely in the area where risks are actually known to exist. The two pending inquiries are precisely the events the carve-out would neutralize. Accepting this change would leave our client without a viable MAE out for the very regulatory developments that are the object of the disclosed inquiries. Under the firm standard and internal playbook, this form of carve-out — one that tracks a known and disclosed adverse development — is not market standard and should be resisted.

Recommended position. REJECT. The MAE carve-out for regulatory action of the kind at issue is rejected. It is overbroad and, critically, intersects the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7, which would otherwise be the primary basis for asserting an MAE. If the counterparty persists on carve-outs for regulatory action generally, at a minimum the carve-out must exclude (or be qualified so as not to cover) the regulatory inquiries and developments disclosed on Schedule 3.7, and should be subject to a "disproportionate effect" or materiality trigger consistent with firm precedent. As drafted, it is unacceptable.

DEVIATION 3 — New limitation period shortens survival for the core representations

Description. The counterparty introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival window for the core representations.

Reconciliation. Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for the agreement. The markup's shortened limitation period directly contradicts the survival matrix in Exhibit B, which controls over general statements in the base materials. Shortening survival for the core representations compresses the client's time to bring claims for breaches of those foundational representations, materially narrowing a standard protection.

Under the controlling partner instruction, any reduction in the survival period for the core representations is treated as a walk-away issue for our client. This is not a concession point. The shortened period conflicts with the governing Exhibit B survival matrix and cannot be accepted.

Recommended position. REJECT (WALK-AWAY ISSUE). Any reduction in the survival period for the core representations is a walk-away item per the controlling partner instruction. The firm-standard survival matrix reflected in Exhibit B must be restored. This should be treated as a firm, non-negotiable point in any further exchange with the counterparty.

IV. SUMMARY RECOMMENDATION TABLE

Deviation                                        Recommendation
1a. Indemnification cap reduction                REJECT (restore firm-standard cap)
1b. Basket conversion (deductible → tipping)     CONCEDE (per controlling instruction)
2.  MAE carve-out for regulatory action          REJECT (qualify to preserve Schedule 3.7 protection)
3.  Survival-period reduction for core reps      REJECT (WALK-AWAY issue; restore Exhibit B matrix)

V. ADDITIONAL NOTES AND NEGOTIATION GUIDANCE

• Sequencing. The client should lead with the conceded basket conversion (Deviation 1b) as a goodwill concession, while holding firm on the survival matrix (Deviation 3), which is a walk-away point. The MAE carve-out (Deviation 2) and the cap reduction (Deviation 1a) should be grouped and pushed back together, as both relate to disclosed exposures (Schedules 3.7 and 5.2).

• Regulatory framework. Consistent with the applicable investment-advisory regulatory framework, our client's disclosures (including the pending regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7) and retained-liability profile (Schedule 5.2) must be preserved. The counterparty's carve-out and cap changes would erode those protections, and the survival reduction would undermine the client's ability to enforce the core representations. Each is inconsistent with the standards applicable to this agreement type.

• Documentation of evidence. The reconciliation relies on: (i) counterparty markup (Deviation source); (ii) base deal materials and firm standard; (iii) Schedules and exhibits (Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, Exhibit B), which control over general statements; and (iv) the controlling latest partner instruction regarding the concession on the basket and the walk-away posture on survival.

VI. CONCLUSION

The counterparty's markup introduces three classes of deviation. The basket conversion (Deviation 1b) is a favorable, conceded change. The indemnification cap reduction (Deviation 1a), the MAE regulatory-action carve-out (Deviation 2), and the survival reduction for the core representations (Deviation 3) all erode core client protections, conflict with the controlling schedules and exhibits, and must be rejected. The survival-period reduction is a firm walk-away issue per the controlling partner instruction. Counsel should advance the negotiated positions set forth above and promptly return a revised agreement.

Prepared by the Funds & Asset Management Practice Group.
